context_blurb:
Snap a celery stick or sniff a rose, and you are handling the parts of a plant. A flowering plant works like a team. Its roots work underground, its stem holds it up, its leaves catch light, and its flowers make seeds. Together, the parts keep the plant alive and start new plants.

Roots grip the soil so the plant stays put. Roots also take in water and minerals from the soil, soaking them up like a sponge. Tiny hairs near each root's tip give it a far bigger surface for drinking. Minerals are not food, though. Roots live in the dark, and a plant makes its food up in its leaves, where light reaches.

A stem holds the leaves up toward the light. Inside it run bundles of tiny tubes. One set of tubes, called xylem, carries water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves and flowers. A second set, called phloem, carries sugar made in the leaves to the rest of the plant. Stand a white carnation in water tinted with blue food dye, and by the next day its petals show blue streaks, because the dyed water climbed up through the xylem.

To make food, a leaf needs carbon dioxide, a gas from the air. Under a microscope, a leaf's underside shows tiny holes called stomata, from the Greek word for mouths. Two bean-shaped cells sit around each hole like a pair of lips, opening it or pressing it shut. Gases pass through the stomata: carbon dioxide comes in, while oxygen and water vapour go out. Light needs no hole, because it shines straight through the leaf's clear skin.

Flowers are the parts that make seeds. Bright petals, sweet scents and nectar draw in visitors. When a bee sips nectar, a fine powder called pollen sticks to its fuzzy body, and some of it brushes off on another flower of its kind. Carrying pollen to a flower of the same kind is called pollination, and it must happen before seeds can form. Butterflies, birds, bats and the wind carry pollen too. Spreading the seeds is a different job that comes later.

After pollination, part of the flower grows into a fruit around the new seeds. To a scientist, a fruit is any part that grows from a flower and holds seeds, so an acorn, with its seed inside a hard shell, is the fruit of an oak. Acorns and maple helicopters are not sweet, but both grew from flowers. A pine cone holds seeds too, yet pines have no flowers, so a cone is not a fruit.

A fruit also helps its seeds travel, so they need not fight the parent plant for water and light. Dandelion seeds float off on fluffy parachutes, and hooked burrs catch in animals' fur. A coconut goes to sea: its husk is full of air pockets, so it floats, and ocean currents carry it to far shores while the seed inside stays alive for months. Animals eat the sweet flesh of berries and spread the seeds, which pass through them unharmed and drop out in their droppings, often far away. The sweet flesh is there to tempt the animals, not to feed the parent plant.

Every seed holds a tiny young plant, a store of food and a tough skin, the seed coat. Soak a dry bean overnight and peel it, and it splits into two fat halves around a tiny plant. These halves are the bean's seed leaves, packed with food that the parent plant stored there. They feed the young plant as it starts to grow, until its own leaves can make food in the light.

To watch a seed sprout, wrap a bean in a wet paper towel inside a glass jar. Within a few days the bean swells and its coat splits. The young root comes out first and grows down, ready to anchor the seedling and drink in water. Only then does the shoot, the young stem with its first leaves, climb toward the light.
